name: Acetyl dipeptide-1 cetyl ester

lead: Acetyl dipeptide-1 cetyl ester, marketed as Calmosensine, is a peptide derivative used in soothing skincare for sensitive, stinging-prone skin, and it appears in some dermatology-brand soothing creams. People use it for less stinging and redness and a calmer, more comfortable complexion.

It is proposed to increase POMC expression, raising alpha-MSH and beta-endorphin, which lowers CGRP release and so reduces nerve-driven stinging and inflammation. Supplier studies report reduced heat perception and improved comfort. A 2016 split-face capsaicin test in 31 women found no significant effect of a finished product containing it versus a comparator cream, and the review notes the product bases differed. It appeared in about 5.7 percent of 88 sensitive-skin products surveyed.

paras: It is used in leave-on soothing creams and serums for reactive skin as part of a gentle daily routine.
No specific adverse events are reported in the review, which cites supplier safety data and CIR assessments. It is a cosmetic ingredient.

angle.text: Acetyl dipeptide-1 cetyl ester (Calmosensine) is used in sensitive-skin products to reduce stinging and redness for a calmer complexion. It is proposed to lower nerve-driven irritation. Supplier data report comfort benefits, while a 2016 capsaicin test of one product found no significant effect.

lead: Acetyl dipeptide-1 cetyl ester, sold to formulators as Calmosensine or Neurosensine, is a synthetic peptide derivative used in soothing creams for sensitive, easily irritated skin. Its chemical name is N-acetyl-L-tyrosyl-L-arginine hexadecyl ester, and it is built from the dipeptide Tyr-Arg attached to a fatty alcohol that makes it more lipophilic, which is intended to help it enter the skin.[1]

Its appearance benefit is meant to be indirect: by easing stinging, heat and discomfort, it aims to leave skin looking calmer and less reactive, so people with sensitive skin can keep using their routines.[1][2] Sensitive skin is common; the introduction of one dermatology paper says more than 50 percent of adults report it.[3]

The proposed mechanism runs through melanocortin and opioid signalling rather than direct action on the heat and pain receptor TRPV1. The supporting data come mostly from supplier studies and patents, and one head-to-head capsaicin test of a finished product found no significant calming effect versus a comparator cream.[1][2][4]
infobox: Derived from the dipeptide Tyr-Arg; synthesis described in a 1998 patent
La Roche-Posay Toleriane Ultra Intense Soothing Care

paras: The ingredient is based on the Tyr-Arg dipeptide, which the literature links to muscle-relaxing and decontracting effects. In the synthesis described in the review, L-arginine hydrochloride is esterified with hexadecanol, a fatty alcohol, which makes the molecule more lipophilic and is said to aid skin penetration; N-acetyl-L-tyrosine is then activated and coupled to the arginine ester. The scheme is traced to a 1998 patent.[1]

The review reports no direct action on TRPV1, the heat- and capsaicin-sensitive receptor involved in stinging. The proposed route is that the peptide increases expression of the POMC gene, whose product is processed into alpha-MSH, ACTH and beta-endorphin.[1]

Alpha-MSH acts on melanocortin receptors and is said to reduce inflammation by modulating NF-kB, while beta-endorphin is said to reduce release of CGRP, a neuropeptide that activates TRPV1 and drives neurogenic inflammation. The proposed result is less stinging and inflammation from heat, capsaicin and mechanical stress.[1] In vitro results cited in the review include raised expression of aquaporin-3, filaggrin, caspase 14 and keratin 10, which the review links to epidermal barrier function, and reduced PGE2 secretion and NF-kB signalling.[1]

The ingredient appears in facial products marketed for sensitive skin. A 2021 survey of 88 facial cosmetics from multinational brands found peptides in 17 percent of products, and acetyl dipeptide-1 cetyl ester was the most common peptide, appearing in roughly five products. Other peptides in the survey included palmitoyl tripeptide-8, acetyl tetrapeptide-15 and palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7.[1][4]

Efficacy data for these peptides sit mostly in patents and supplier brochures rather than randomised placebo-controlled studies, and acetyl dipeptide-1 cetyl ester is the only one among them with a clinical study that included volunteers with sensitive skin.[1][4] A separate 2022 survey of 88 sensitive-skin products from 19 multinational brands ranked niacinamide, Avena sativa, allantoin and glycyrrhetinic acid among the most common actives and described clinical studies on these ingredients as sparse and of limited methodological quality.[5]

Supplier-reported studies cited in the review include a 3 percent cream tested on 21 volunteers, in which the ability to distinguish between warm, hot, very hot and painful heat levels was reduced, and a double-blind split-hand study of 18 volunteers in which the treated hand felt more comfortable after sandpaper abrasion.[1] The supplier concludes that the ingredient may ease some unpleasant sensations linked to sensitive skin.[1]

An independent comparison is described under Clinical studies. The review cautions that differences between the product bases could affect the result, so it does not establish that one ingredient is better than the other.[1] The authors call for more rigorous randomised clinical studies, and treat the number of patents on sensitive-skin products containing the ingredient as a sign of industry interest rather than proof of efficacy.[1]

The review reports no specific adverse events and cites manufacturer safety data sheets and the Cosmetic Ingredient Review for topical safety, with no further safety data for this ingredient.[1] It is a cosmetic ingredient rather than a drug.

The ingredient is used in dermatology-brand soothing creams, and the capsaicin study identified one such product by name, a La Roche-Posay Toleriane cream.[2] Cosmetic ingredient peptides in general are marketed for their potency at low dosage and ability to interact with skin cells by several mechanisms.[4]

A single-blind, randomised split-face capsaicin-stinging test enrolled 31 women aged 19 to 65 with self-perceived sensitive to very sensitive skin. After a three-day period without facial products and a positive reaction to a 40 ppm capsaicin cream, each test product was applied to one nasolabial fold; burning was rated immediately and at 1, 2, 5, 10 and 15 minutes. It compared Eucerin UltraSensitive Soothing Care (4-t-butylcyclohexanol) with La Roche-Posay Toleriane Ultra Intense Soothing Care (acetyl dipeptide-1 cetyl ester).[2]

All 31 subjects reported stinging after capsaicin, and the 4-t-butylcyclohexanol product gave significantly lower burning at one and two minutes after application than the acetyl dipeptide-1 cetyl ester product.[2] A companion 2016 paper found in vitro that 4-t-butylcyclohexanol reduced TRPV1 activation while acetyl dipeptide-1 cetyl ester had no effect on the receptor, and it also tested the ingredients' effects on PGE2 release and NF-kB activation.[3] The supplier studies described above are the other human data.
